description: Three Marsketeers in roles of : A Mission Director, a Design & Engineering expert, and a Modern Software Specialist united by a single mission: "All for one, and every astronaut home."
summary:
Up to 22 light-minutes from Earth with no GPS or emergency extraction, Martian astronauts need to be completely self-sufficient to survive. 
HALO Mars (Hazard Aware Layered Operations on Mars) is an interactive, real-time 3D navigation tool that answers one critical question: Can the crew still get home? Astronauts cannot rely on geographic distance alone to estimate how far they can explore from base. The walk back can cost far more oxygen and energy than the trek out once steep climbs, loose sand, sample weight, headwinds, and solar storms are included. They need a multidimensional approach to identify the weakest link before their safety envelope is breached. 
HALO Mars fuses five NASA datasets: HiRISE/MOLA slope, THEMIS sand and cold, CRISM sample targets, MEDA wind, and RAD radiation with DONKI solar storm alerts, alongside the astronaut’s heart rate, payload mass, and remaining oxygen, battery, and calories.
Its dual-pass route solver scores the outbound and the return cost on the terrain grid, then paints a live Point of Safe Return: a green safe zone, an amber caution band, and a red turn-back region. A 360°horizon skyline matcher provides a GPS-free position approximation on Mars.
details:
Live Point of Safe Return: Replaces a standard circular distance radius with a dynamic, terrain-aware safe-return envelope and a lowest-energy return corridor computed in real time. Outbound cost and return cost are scored separately.

  • Multi-mission NASA data fusion in a single pane of glass:
    • HiRISE / MOLA: Elevation, slope gradients, and geotechnical cliff barriers.
    • THEMIS: Thermal inertia differentiating loose drift sand from bedrock.
    • CRISM: Mineralogical targets coupled with geological sample mass.
    • REMS / MEDA: Katabatic wind drag along the walking direction.
    • RAD and DONKI: Background radiation and canyon sky-view shielding, plus a solar energetic particle (SEP) alert that raises the dose when the feed is up.
  • Biophysical data fusion: Simulates partial-gravity locomotion and NASA-STD-3001 limits, flagging the critical health bottlenecks using heart rate, blood oxygen, core temperature, and thermal strain parameters.
  • Optical navigation: A 360° skyline match estimates position and heading without GPS.

Few interesting concepts done as part this hackathon are- 

  • HALO Mars reimagines planetary cartography from static geographic distance to a dynamic survival distance.
  • It turns those  complex calculations into  clear boundaries on the Martian map .
  • Dual-use case: This same turnaround concept could support backcountry hiking, rescue, alpine mountaineering, and wildland firefighting on earth if USGS slope, footing or snow, and NOAA wind replace the Mars layers.
  • HALO Mars is also our nod to saying 'Hello, Mars ! . As humans when we greet a new world and make it home, we have to make sure every explorer is safe in each part of this journey.

Tools, languages, and software:

  • Languages and architecture: Native JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS, run in the browser.
  • 3D visualization: Three.js WebGL2 terrain rendering of the Mars surface.
  • APIs and hardware: Web Bluetooth API (GATT heart-rate straps), DeviceOrientation API (IMU compass heading), NASA JPL Mars Trek WMTS, and NASA CCMC DONKI REST API.
  • SI tools: Gemini, Cursor, Devin
  • Routes export as GeoJSON and CSV.

This tool was designed with following factors in consideration:

  • Survival is not distance alone. The limit needs real-time adjustment from external terrain and weather and from the crew’s physiology.
  • A clear interface so mission planners and astronauts can read the safe, caution, and turn-back bands.
  • Low energy cost: in an emergency the map rendering can be disabled, so that the remaining application can work with very limited power.
  • Martian parameters and sites are bound to published data for Mount Sharp and Jezero, with Mars Trek imagery and DONKI alerts used when those feeds respond.
